questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The Canadian nature in British Columbia because Canada was open after the pandemic.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was very easy. UBC provided us with very detailed emails with guides to find all neccessary information.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I was a law student so I was not allowed to participate in the GoGlobal orientation week provided by the university. However, Allard Law sent us with written information both before and at arrival.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: It was for many other students extremely hard unless you wanted to pay around 9-12,000 DKK each month. I lived with my boyfriend in an apartment where we knew the owners before arrival.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Living off campus is a good idea if you want to explore the city more. Campus is located around 30-45 min in bus from Campus, so many students on campus spent most of the time there. Campus is very big and around 100,000 people live there which means it is almost a city in itself. Therefore, students living on campus had everything they needed there. Living off campus gives a lot of extra opportunities to see other parts of the city. The only minus about living off campus is the unreliable bus system with busses from time to time were a "no show".

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer:
My registration process was different then the other exchange students' because I was a law student. I can therefore only provide information regarding the registration process for law students. It is a very stressful registration system before arrival because you register for courses 2 times. The first round is in June, where you are only allowed to register for 2 courses. In the next round you can register for the remaining courses you need to get full credits. Please remember that it is first come, first serve so you need to be ready at the exact time and even there I did not get the courses I wanted. It is your own responsibility that the courses you take not overlap both regarding the exam date and the weekly schedule. As a difference from University of Copenhagen, classes are mandatory to attend, and you often get graded for your attentance, so it is quite important that your classes do not overlap. 

Don't stress if you do not get the courses you wanted! The first couple of weeks of classes you are allowed to switch courses and normally people have registered for more courses then they need, so you can continue to check if the courses you want get available spots.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: We had a exchange counselor at Allard Law, who helped us if we had any questions in the registration process.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: It was not very succesful. The local students can choose courses prior to exchange students and the registration process is very stressful which means that I ended up with only 1 of the courses I initially wanted.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: If you want very specific courses you need to me very fast in the first registration. Otherwise check several times a day when classes begin if people should drop the course. In general my best advice is to be flexible about the courses you want and pay attention to the exam form. The exam period is only 2 weeks and begins immediately after classes end. I had only one course with final exam, where the others were final papers you could write during the term. That made the exam period a lot less stressful and I could enjoy December more.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: I was master student at UCPH but were only allowed to attend BA courses at UBC, again because I was law student. Futhermore, I could only choose Level 300 and Level 400 courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The courses I had were seminars (fewer students and more attentance required). Compared to style of teaching at UCPH the professors demand more attentance in class.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
International environmental law 
Introduction to Asian Legal Systems
Japanese Business Law

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend courses with a final paper as exam form. I really liked International Environmental law.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: Canada has the most expensive phone bills in the world where the cheapest start around 400 DKK for 10 GB a month. Furthermore, food is crazy expensive! You would pay 3-4 times more for especially fresh fruit and vegetables compared to Denmark. Living is also really expensive. Even on campus for a shared room with 5 others they paid around 5,500 DKK.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Living, phone bills, and food in general were much more expensive than expected. Going out for dinner (especially sushi) was cheaper.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Everything! UBC has over 600 clubs.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I joined the exchange club and the UBC triathlon club which I really enjoyed. I would recommend the exchange club no matter what your hobbies because they arrange multiple activities each month only for exchange students. I know other exchange students really liked the VOC club.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: We did a lot of travelling both in BC and in North America in general. I arrived two 3 weeks prior to school start and had 2,5 weeks vacation in the Rockies first and then in Whistler, which I can really recommend. Also if you are into hiking, the app "Alltrails" is very helpful so we went on hikes almost every weekend. I also visited Toronto, Vancouver Island, Hawaii and San Franscisco during the term because I only had classes Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: It was very easy because Vancouver is very multi cultural.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: It is in general hard socializing with local students because you are only there for 4 month. I joined to triathlon club which almost only consisted of local students and that was a great way to socialize with the locals. My best tip would therefore be to join some of the clubs on campus.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: None.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: The multi cultural society.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Enjoy the nature and arrive 2-4 weeks before so you have time to travel around in the beautiful country.
Be open to new cultures, because Vancouver is a very multi cultural city where no culture is a majority culture. 
Socialize a lot in the beginning and prioritize the social activities so you quickly can make friends.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember rain clothes!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: How much I learned about other cultures being abroad.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: I did not have any great challenges.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
